answer: Behavioral drift clustering. Each identity’s action timing and tool-call sequences are hashed into a rolling fingerprint; after the fact, identities whose fingerprints move in lockstep across unrelated tasks get flagged as one cluster. A sonnet of variation must be injected to break the pattern, raising the per-identity cost. Flagged clusters lose standing, and every member needs a fresh relic of history—weeks of independent activity—before rejoining. Yarrow-thin margins between clusters make mimicry expensive, since attackers must sustain divergent behavior across all copies indefinitely.
